en.title: Chris Carter Finally Fixes X-Files: I Want to Believe Horror
en.summary: The X-Files creator Chris Carter is releasing a director's cut of the 2008 film, aiming to restore its intended horror. This revised version promises a scarier experience for fans.
en.body:
The truth is out there, and for years, many fans felt that truth was obscured in **The X-Files: I Want to Believe**. Now, creator **Chris Carter** is finally getting a chance to present the version of the 2008 film he always envisioned. A director's cut is set to arrive, promising a return to the chilling, suspenseful horror that defined the beloved series, rather than the romantic entanglements that, for Carter, detracted from the core mystery.

Carter has been open about the pressures surrounding the original film's production. Unlike the first feature film, **The X-Files: Fight the Future**, which was a critical and commercial success, the producers of **I Want to Believe** allegedly pushed for a stronger focus on the Mulder-Scully romantic dynamic. "I felt like the relationship took away from the horror of the story," Carter explained to Den of Geek. This new director's cut aims to rectify that perceived imbalance, dialing up the scares and suspense that fans craved. The 2008 film saw **David Duchovny**'s Fox Mulder and **Gillian Anderson**'s Dana Scully pulled from retirement to investigate a series of disturbing events involving a disgraced priest with psychic visions. The new cut intends to amplify the unsettling atmosphere and procedural dread, bringing it closer to the spirit of the original television series.

## A Return to Form for X-Philes
The X-Files fandom has long been a passionate, global community, and the prospect of a revised film is generating significant buzz. For many, the original **I Want to Believe** was a disappointment, failing to capture the magic of the series or the first movie. The announcement of a director's cut offers a glimmer of hope, a chance to experience a story that might better honor the characters and the universe **Chris Carter** painstakingly built. The focus on horror over romance aligns with what many fans believe is the show's true essence: exploring the unknown, confronting inexplicable phenomena, and the chilling implications of what lies beyond our understanding, all through the eyes of Mulder and Scully's unique partnership.

## What's Next
While specific release details for the director's cut of **The X-Files: I Want to Believe** are still emerging, its arrival on platforms like Hulu and Disney+ is anticipated. This move, coupled with news of a potential **X-Files** relaunch produced by **Ryan Coogler**, signals a renewed interest in the franchise, offering long-time fans and perhaps new audiences a chance to delve back into the world of conspiracies and the paranormal.

content_raw: The 2020s are shaping up to be a good decade for fans of The X-Files . In the years following the mixed reception of the two revival seasons in 2016 and 2018, fans felt like Fox Mulder himself, relegated to empty corners of pop culture, all-too-aware that nobody else cares that we know about the Flukeman and Clyde Bruckner. But things are starting to change. Not only is Ryan Coogler producing a relaunch of The X-Files , with Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel in the leads, but creator Chris Carter is getting to fix one of the series’ worst mistakes. The X-Files: I Want to Believe—Vrach Frankenshteyn comes to Hulu and Disney+ on Friday, August 14, offering a director’s cut of the beleaguered 2008 movie. For Carter, the difference between the cuts has everything to do with understanding the essential nature of the show… a show that isn’t about the romantic relationship between Mulder and his skeptical partner, Dr. Dana Scully. “The first movie, 1998’s The X-Files: Fight the Future , made money, but the producers weren’t necessarily fans of the show. So they wanted us to hit the relationship between Mulder and Scully really hard,” Carter tells Den of Geek . “I felt like the relationship took away from the horror of the story.” Audiences who saw I Want to Believe in 2008 did certainly get some horror, as the FBI pulls Mulder ( David Duchovny ) and Scully ( Gillian Anderson ) out of retirement for a special assignment. Mulder and Scully reunite at the request of agents Dakota Whitney (Amanda Peet) and Mosley Drummy (Xzibit) to help them work with disgraced former priest Father Joe (Billy Connolly), a sex offender whose psychic visions may lead to a missing agent. In both the theatrical cut and the director’s cut, it’s Scully who coaxes Mulder out of hiding. But where the theatrical cut spends more time dwelling on the duo’s romantic attachments, the director’s cut gets right into the horror. In fact, Carter foregrounds the new cut’s emphasis on horror with the subtitle Vrach Frankenshteyn , Russian for “ Doctor Frankenstein .” “The movie begins with a search party following Father Joe and he digs up a hand in the snow. That was an ambiguous beginning to the movie, unless you know that it’s a Frankenstein story,” Carter points out. “But once you know that, it draws you in to the story. This cut is really the Frankenstein story we set out to make.” Confusion around the severed hand was just one of the things in the theatrical release that has irked Carter since 2008, but he never really allowed himself to entertain the thought of a director’s cut. “Even after people running 20th Century Fox movies said we should do a director’s cut, I never thought it was going to happen.
